What this page does not claim

  • No confirmed planet. Every dip, signal and feed entry here is a candidate, unconfirmed. Passing vetting is not a confirmation. The match with pi Men c says the planet is already known, not that this run confirmed it.
  • No planet sizes. No stellar radius is stored, so a depth gives only a planet-to-star radius ratio. The Planets page shows the working.
  • No people on the panel. The panel is the Sentinels and the Probes: 2 Sentinels and 3 Probes. Sentinels run on Claude (Anthropic) by default; other providers are supported and labelled. Probes are deterministic matched-filter detectors. Their weights rest on calibration with 10 planted and 10 empty light curves each, so they are rough.
  • Archive values only. This page claims no detection. A TOI or archive match compares a stored period with published values.
  • No image of the planet. The planet on the Overview is an artist's impression; the field stars on the sky map are decorative.

Sky

Twenty-six days of pi Men.
One planet found again. One dip unexplained.

3,485 stored brightness measurements over 26.0 days. The panel, 2 Sentinels and 3 Probes (no people), marked 7 dips, which the vetting code grouped into 3 signals: 1 passed, 1 flagged, 1 rejected. Each dip is this pipeline's own candidate, unconfirmed as an independent detection; the archive match says the planet is already known, not that this run confirmed it. The stored archive cross-match (docs/results/pi_men_crossmatch.json) finds the lead signal consistent with pi Men c, a published planet: a known planet, not a discovery. Archive values only. This page claims no detection.

Data: The Extrasolar Planets Encyclopaedia (exoplanet.eu), fetched 18 Oct 2026; 8,049 planets with a stored distance, around 5,433 stars. https://exoplanet.eu/catalog/. NASA Exoplanet Archive not used: HTTP Error 400: Bad Request. exoplanet.eu lists as confirmed every object it treats as a planet: bodies up to 60 Jupiter masses (within their uncertainty), published or announced. Its list is broader than the NASA Exoplanet Archive's, which keeps objects up to 30 Jupiter masses from refereed papers. The list includes 9 entries exoplanet.eu names as exocomets. 327 of its 8,376 planets have no stored distance and are not plotted.

        
Not plotted. The feed's stars (TIC 348835438, TIC 349088467, TIC 348770361) have no stored positions, so they are not on this map. pi Men is placed from the dataset, like every other star; pi Men c is the planet SetuHQ's run recovered.

        
How to read it. Positions: heliocentric galactic coordinates from RA, Dec (J2000) and distance; x points to the Galactic centre and the grid is the Galactic plane. Axis ticks are in light-years (1 pc = 3.262 ly). Colour: the detection method of the earliest planet shown for each star (Method: the first detection method the source lists for the planet.). Size: planets per star. Microlensing distances come from models of each event and are uncertain (how microlensing works). The bias in the cloud is where surveys looked and what each method can see, not where planets are. The Milky Way is an artist's impression drawn by the page, not data; the Sun's position in it is approximate.

        
How we classify: by radius when exoplanet.eu gives one, in Earth radii (1 RJ = 11.21 R⊕): Earth-size below 1.25, super-Earth 1.25–2, sub-Neptune 2–4, Neptune-like 4–10, gas giant 10 or more. Without a radius, by mass (or m sin i, a minimum mass) in Earth masses (1 MJ = 317.8 M⊕): Earth-size below 2, super-Earth 2–10, Neptune-like 10–50, gas giant 50 or more. With neither, the class is shown as a dash.

Sentinels and Probes
Five reviewers.
Each one earns its vote.

        
The panel that marked dips in run tess-pi-men-s1: the Sentinels and the Probes, no people. Sentinels run on Claude (Anthropic) by default; other providers are supported and labelled. Probes are deterministic matched-filter detectors.

        

      

      

        
        

      

      

      
Sentinels run on Claude (Anthropic) by default; other providers are supported and labelled. Probes are deterministic matched-filter detectors. Weights come from 10 planted and 10 empty light curves each: too few to separate 0.6 from 0.5.

      
Measured on real TOIs
The live feed's new signals are consistent with noise. Noise alone should give about 12.3 false new_candidate signals per 100 targets reviewed, against 15.8 per 100 on the live feed. Under that earlier rule a new_candidate on the feed was more likely noise than a signal.
The feed's stricter rule, pre-registered and measured again on this code. The signal must now pass in both reviewed sectors with a FAP below 0.001 over 2,000 trials. On the held-out half, noise alone gives 6.1 false signals per 100 targets (95% CI 4.0–9.4), down from 27.8 (23.1–33.1). That is still far above the 1.6 new signals per 100 targets the real light curves give, so the feed is still dominated by false alarms, and feed-level completeness fell from 39% to 17%. A feed admission is a lead for human or follow-up review, not a candidate of any confirmed status. Re-run on this code, the live feed's 19 targets admit 0 new signals.
Measured on a stated benchmark, not discoveries. 300 confirmed or known planets (CP/KP), 300 false positives and 62 false alarms from the TOI table (fetched 2026-10-19, seed 20261019), one TOI per star; held-out half shown. Panel: the three Probes (deterministic detectors) with their frozen calibrated weights; sector-wide BLS; vetting; limb-darkened fit; the feed-level table adds the feed's FAP (200 trials).

Weights. A reviewer's weight is its calibration skill from injection tests: the true-positive rate on injected transits minus the false-positive rate on empty light curves, floored (calibrate.py). The calibrated weights are stored in docs/results/reviewer_weights_full_panel.json. The weight in this run is the one manifest.json records; when it differs from the calibrated weight, the run did not use the calibrated weights.

Chapter 1 of 15
How a survey works

      
A survey points a camera at many stars at once and measures each one's brightness again and again. Most stars never show a planet. Only planets whose orbits happen to line up with us can cross their star's face.

      
      

        
Why only a few transit

        
A planet transits only if its orbit is aligned closely enough with our line of sight. For random orientations the chance is about R★/a, the star's radius over the orbit's size (Winn 2010). Close-in planets around large stars transit more often.

Transit ›
Chapter 2 of 15 · SetuHQ does this
Transit

      
When a planet crosses its star, it blocks a little light. The dip's depth gives the planet's size relative to the star; its repetition gives the period. This is what SetuHQ does: its run found pi Men c's transits in TESS sector 1. Open SetuHQ's Transit case ›

      
      

        
What shapes the dip

        
The depth is roughly (Rp/R★)². The star is brighter at its centre than its edge (limb darkening), so the bottom of the dip is rounded, not flat, and a central crossing dips deeper than k² (Mandel & Agol 2002; Claret 2017 coefficients for TESS). The four contact points set the total duration T14 and the flat-bottom duration T23 (Winn 2010).

‹ How a survey worksToward and away ›
Chapter 3 of 15
Toward and away

      
Light from a star moving toward us arrives slightly bluer; moving away, slightly redder. Only the motion along our line of sight shifts the light. Motion across the sky (proper motion) shifts nothing.

      
      

        
How small the shift is

        
Δλ/λ = v_r/c, with v_r positive for motion away (redshift). For a wobble of tens of m/s the shift is a ten-millionth of the wavelength, so spectrographs measure it by cross-correlating thousands of lines (Fischer et al. 2016). The star's colour does not visibly change.

‹ TransitRadial velocity ›
Chapter 4 of 15
Radial velocity

      
A planet and its star both orbit their shared centre of mass, the barycentre. The star's small orbit makes its light shift back and forth: the radial-velocity curve. Its amplitude K gives the planet's minimum mass, m sin i.

      
      

        
The numbers

        
K = (2πG/P)^⅓ · Mp sin i / (M★ + Mp)^⅔ / √(1 − e²) (Gaudi & Winn 2007). The star's orbit is a★ = a · Mp/(M★ + Mp); the planet's is a · M★/(M★ + Mp). Eccentric orbits follow Kepler's equation, M = E − e sin E. Masses use the IAU nominal GM values (Prša et al. 2016).

Why Earth twins are hard

        
An Earth twin moves its Sun-like star by about 9 cm/s. ESPRESSO holds better than 25 cm/s within a night and about 50 cm/s over months (Pepe et al. 2021). The star's own surface (granulation, oscillations, spots) adds RV noise of order m/s (Fischer et al. 2016), larger than the signal itself.

Chapter 5 of 15
Astrometry

      
The star's small orbit also moves its position on the sky. Astrometry measures that tiny loop, which gives the orbit's tilt and so the planet's true mass. The signal grows with the planet's mass and orbit and shrinks with distance.

      
      

        
α = (Mp/M★)(a/d): the star's angular orbit, in arcseconds for a in AU and d in parsecs (Perryman et al. 2014). A wobble consistent with an orbiting companion becomes a planet only when its mass is pinned below the planetary limit, usually with RV as well, as for Gaia-4b (Stefánsson et al. 2025). Gaia ended science observations in January 2025; its fourth data release, planned for December 2026, carries the epoch astrometry.

        
The drawing is an illustration: its scales are chosen to show the three motions apart, and the planet's wobble is enlarged and labelled. It quotes no Gaia measurement precision: the project's research atlas holds no sourced per-measurement figure for Gaia DR3, so none is given here.

‹ Radial velocityMicrolensing ›
Chapter 6 of 15
Microlensing

      
When a foreground star (the lens) passes almost in front of a background star (the source), its gravity bends and magnifies the source's light for days to weeks. A planet around the lens adds a short extra spike. The lens itself is often too faint to see.

      
      

        
Point-lens magnification: A(u) = (u² + 2)/(u√(u² + 4)), with u the lens–source separation in Einstein radii; A(1) = 1.342. The Einstein angle is θ_E = √(κ M π_rel), κ ≈ 8.14 mas/M☉ (Gaudi 2012). A planetary spike lasts about √q · t_E, where q is the planet-to-star mass ratio. An event never repeats, so the planet cannot be re-observed this way.

‹ AstrometryBlocking starlight ›
Chapter 7 of 15
Blocking starlight

      
To photograph a planet, the starlight must be blocked. A Jupiter twin reflects about a billionth of its Sun's visible light; an Earth twin about 10⁻¹⁰ (Lawson et al. 2013). Young giant planets glow in the infrared and are far easier, which is why imaging finds young, wide, massive planets.

      
      

        
Blocking starlight

        
    
          
  1. History. Bernard Lyot invented the coronagraph in 1930 to study the Sun's corona without an eclipse; a focal-plane mask blocks the disc and a "Lyot stop" removes the diffracted light (Lyot 1939). SOHO's LASCO coronagraphs show the same idea every day (Brueckner et al. 1995). The Sun scene above is an illustration based on LASCO, not a LASCO image.
    2. 
          
  2. Coronagraph families. Lyot-type amplitude masks, apodised pupils and phase masks such as the vortex. The key figure is the inner working angle, in units of λ/D (Mawet et al. 2012). Earth at 10 pc sits 0.1″ from its star: about 5.3 λ/D for a 6 m telescope at 550 nm [calc].
    3. 
          
  3. Adaptive optics and speckles. A deformable mirror flattens the turbulent wavefront hundreds of times a second. What remains are speckles; angular differential imaging lets the sky rotate while speckles stay fixed, so they can be subtracted (Marois et al. 2006).
    4. 
          
  4. Starshade. A flower-shaped screen flown far in front of a telescope (Cash 2006). The Roman Starshade Rendezvous concept: 26 m at 26,000 km; HabEx: 52 m at about 76,600 km (HabEx Final Report).
    5. 
          
  5. Nulling interferometry. Two telescopes combined half a wave out of phase cancel the star on a dark fringe while an off-axis planet sits on a bright one (Bracewell 1978; the LIFE concept, Quanz et al. 2022).
    6. 
        

        
Coronagraph families, plane by plane

        
Each family below is drawn as four planes of one optical train. The intensities are computed, not painted: Fraunhofer optics of an ideal, monochromatic telescope with a clear circular pupil, shown on a log stretch from the star's peak down to a millionth. The mask and stop sizes, the apodiser and the planets' brightness are illustrative and say so.

        
      

      
      

        
    
          
  1. Lyot coronagraph. An opaque disc in the focal plane blocks the core of the star's image. What it does not remove is the light its edge diffracts, which the next lens sends to the rim of the re-imaged pupil; a Lyot stop slightly smaller than the pupil catches that rim (Lyot 1939). With a 4 λ/D disc, closing the stop from 150% to 80% of the pupil cuts the starlight at 8 λ/D from 6.7×10⁻⁵ to 1.8×10⁻⁷ of the star's peak (no coronagraph: 7.8×10⁻⁵) [calc], while a planet well outside the disc keeps 64% of its light, the stop's area.
    2. 
          
  2. Apodised pupil. Instead of a mask, the pupil's transmission tapers to its edge, so the image has no sharp edge to ring from. For A(ρ) = (1 − ρ²)² the brightest ring near 5 λ/D falls from 7.8×10⁻⁴ to 1.2×10⁻⁶ of the clear pupil's peak [calc], but only 1/(2n + 1) = 20% of the light gets through and the core is wider. Real apodisers (shaped pupils, prolate and APLC designs) are optimised numerically; this taper is illustrative.
    3. 
          
  3. Vortex phase mask. A transparent mask whose phase winds around its centre (e^(2iθ), charge 2) moves an on-axis star's light outside the re-imaged pupil: for an ideal charge-2 vortex on a clear circular aperture the field there is exactly zero inside the pupil and (1/ρ)² outside it [calc], so a stop just inside the pupil removes the star. Phase masks are the family that works closest to the star (Mawet et al. 2012); real vortices leave residuals from wavefront errors and the star's finite size.
    4. 
          
  4. Adaptive optics and ADI. A deformable mirror turns the seeing halo into a sharp core, but quasi-static speckles λ/D wide remain. With the instrument's pupil fixed, the sky and the planet turn through the night while the speckles stay; the median of the sequence models the speckles, and each frame minus it, turned back by its field rotation and stacked, keeps the planet (Marois et al. 2006). The frames on the stage are synthetic. On the sky, GPI reaches about 10⁻⁴ raw contrast at 0.4″ in 60 s and more than ten times deeper after an hour of ADI (Bailey et al. 2016).
    5.

‹ Blocking starlightRadio ›
Chapter 9 of 15
Radio

      
Magnetised planets shine at radio wavelengths: electrons spiralling down field lines into the auroral zones emit by the cyclotron maser, beamed in a hollow cone, up to the local cyclotron frequency (Zarka 1998; Treumann 2006). A close-in planet can also drive such emission on its star, as Io does on Jupiter (Zarka 2007). No exoplanet's own radio emission has been confirmed. Every claim below is tentative or contested, and says so.

      
      

        
The frequency scale

        
The cyclotron maser emits at, and just below, f_ce = eB/(2π m_e) ≈ 2.80 MHz per gauss of field at the source, so the highest frequency seen gives the field there. A weak planetary field emits below tens of MHz, where only low-frequency arrays such as LOFAR (10–240 MHz; van Haarlem et al. 2013) can listen; an M dwarf's kilogauss field reaches GHz.

The claims, and where they stand

        

          
Tentative, not confirmed
τ Boötis b · LOFAR
Circularly polarised bursty emission at 14–21 MHz, about 3σ, with nothing in the off-beams; a slowly varying 21–30 MHz signal was also reported, with the authors' own doubts (Turner et al. 2021). Follow-up LOFAR observations covering 70% of the orbit, including the earlier orbital phases, showed no bursty or slow emission (Turner et al. 2024).
Turner et al. 2021 · Turner et al. 2024

          
Contested: no planet yet explains it
GJ 1151 · LOFAR
Low-frequency emission from a quiet red dwarf, with the character of a planetary aurora, interpreted as the star interacting with an Earth-size planet on a 1–5 day orbit (Vedantham et al. 2020). Radial velocities then found a planet on a 390-day orbit that is very unlikely to be the source, and no short-period planet (minimum mass below 1.2 Earth masses) (Blanco-Pozo et al. 2023).
Vedantham et al. 2020 · Blanco-Pozo et al. 2023

          
Candidate
YZ Ceti · VLA
Coherent bursts at 2–4 GHz, two of them at similar orbital phases of YZ Ceti b, which could plausibly power them; stellar activity is not ruled out, so YZ Ceti is a candidate star–planet-interaction system (Pineda & Villadsen 2023).
Pineda & Villadsen 2023

        

        
Radio found the first planets, another way

        
In 1992, Wolszczan and Frail found planets around the millisecond pulsar PSR B1257+12 from the regular wobble in its pulses' arrival times (Wolszczan & Frail 1992): the planets tug the pulsar, and the light-travel time changes by milliseconds. That is radio timing, not radio from a planet. Its card on the Galaxy tour ›

Not an exoplanet detection method

          
Technosignature searches (SETI)

          
These look for engineered signals, not for planets or their aurorae, and are kept separate here. Breakthrough Listen observed 1,327 nearby stars at 1.10–3.45 GHz with Green Bank and Parkes and, after excluding terrestrial interference, found zero candidates; the upper limits on a transmitter's power are 2×10¹² W and 9×10¹² W (Price et al. 2020; targets from Isaacson et al. 2017).

        
SetuHQ does not observe in radio. The scene is an illustration: field lines, cone and orbit are not to scale, and burst times are illustrative; only the cut-off frequency is computed.

Chapter 11 of 15 · explainer: SetuHQ does not do this
Reading atmospheres

      
During a transit, a sliver of starlight passes through the planet's atmosphere at its edge. Where molecules absorb, the atmosphere is opaque higher up, so the planet looks slightly bigger at those wavelengths. SetuHQ does not do spectroscopy: this explains how JWST-class telescopes read atmospheres.

      
      

        
One scale height H = k_B T/(μ m_H g) of atmosphere changes the transit depth by about 2 H Rp/R★². Strong features span a few scale heights. Hot, puffy, hydrogen-rich planets around small stars give the biggest signals (Seager & Sasselov 2000; Winn 2010).

‹ False positivesMolecules and life ›
Chapter 12 of 15
Molecules and life

      
Each gas absorbs at its own wavelengths. A molecule's shape sets how it vibrates, and its vibrations set where it absorbs in the infrared. No single gas proves life; a biosignature needs context.

      
      

        
A molecule with N atoms has 3N − 6 ways to vibrate (3N − 5 if it is straight): water has three, carbon dioxide four (its bend comes twice, at right angles), methane nine. A mode absorbs infrared light only if it changes the molecule's dipole. That is why CO₂'s symmetric stretch (7.50 µm), O₂'s stretch and two of methane's four fundamentals are silent in the infrared. The bands the modes make are the ones the Reading atmospheres chapter marks: water's two stretches at 2.66 and 2.73 µm make its 2.7 µm band, methane's ν₃ the 3.3 µm band, CO₂'s asymmetric stretch the 4.26 µm band, and CO's stretch the 4.67 µm band.

        
Band positions: the atlas's NIST CCCBDB fundamentals, λ = 10⁴/ν̃. Displacements are symmetry-correct sketches with the centre of mass fixed and no net spin, not a force-field calculation. In every mode the atom that moves most swings 0.2 Å, and the stage states how much that exaggerates its zero-point motion, the root-mean-square displacement from ħ/2ω at the mode's frequency: for water's hydrogens in ν₁ that is 0.047 Å, so they are drawn ×4. Time is slowed 10¹³ to 10¹⁴ times, and the stage gives the factor for each mode.

Biosignature checklist

        
    
          
  1. Detection significance. How many sigma, from how many independent analyses?
    2. 
          
  2. Context. The star, the planet's temperature and the other gases present (Meadows et al. 2018).
    3. 
          
  3. Disequilibrium. Gases that would react away without a source, such as O₂ with CH₄ (Krissansen-Totton et al. 2018).
    4. 
          
  4. Abiotic sources ruled out. Every non-living way to make the gas, checked (Schwieterman et al. 2018; Catling et al. 2018).
    5. 
        

        
No gas has passed this checklist on any planet. Life has not been detected anywhere beyond Earth.

        

          
Phosphine on Venus: contested
2020: phosphine reported in Venus's clouds from JCMT and ALMA (Greaves et al. 2020). Re-analyses found no significant detection (Snellen et al. 2020; Villanueva et al. 2021), with a reply by the original team (Greaves et al. 2021). Still disputed.
  • Greaves et al. 2020, Nat. Astron. 5, 655 (phosphine on Venus)
  • Snellen et al. 2020, A&A 644, L2 (re-analysis)
  • Villanueva et al. 2021, Nat. Astron. 5, 631
  • Greaves et al. 2021, reply
  • Bains et al. 2021, Astrobiology 21, 1277

          
DMS on K2-18 b: tentative, debated
2023: methane and CO₂ in an H₂-rich atmosphere, with "potential signs" of DMS (Madhusudhan et al. 2023). 2025: a ~3σ MIRI feature consistent with DMS and/or DMDS (Madhusudhan et al. 2025). Independent analyses found insufficient evidence (Schmidt et al. 2025; Luque et al. 2025). Not established.
  • Madhusudhan et al. 2023, ApJL 956, L13 (K2-18 b)
  • Madhusudhan et al. 2025, ApJL 983, L40
  • Schmidt et al. 2025, re-analysis (arXiv:2501.18477)
  • Luque et al. 2025, joint analysis (arXiv:2505.13407)

‹ Reading atmospheresPopulation ›
Chapter 13 of 15
Population

      
With thousands of planets, patterns appear. Two of them: a valley in the sizes of small planets, and the zone around each star where liquid water could last.

      
      

        
Small close-in planets come in two groups: rocky super-Earths below about 1.5 R⊕ and gas-wrapped sub-Neptunes around 2–3 R⊕, with fewer in between (Fulton et al. 2017 found at least a factor-of-two deficit at 1.5–2.0 R⊕ in a carefully measured sample). The leading explanations strip thin envelopes from small cores: photoevaporation (Owen & Wu 2017) or core-powered mass loss (Gupta & Schlichting 2019).

        
These are raw catalogue counts (planets with a stored radius and period < 100 d; 40 log bins from 0.5 to 20 Earth radii), not occurrence rates: nothing corrects for which planets are easier to find, and catalogue radii carry the stars' radius errors. The dip is shallower here than in Fulton et al.'s corrected, precise sample. pi Men c's stored radius is 1.87 R⊕.

      

      
      

        
The habitable zone is the range of starlight in which an Earth-like planet could keep liquid surface water. Its limits come from climate models as a flux that depends on the star's temperature (Kopparapu et al. 2014). Being in it is necessary, not sufficient: it says nothing about a planet's atmosphere, and many planets inside it are giants.

Chapter 14 of 15
Equations of life

      
The Drake and Seager equations are ways to organise what we do not know. They are speculative frameworks, not predictions: no number on this page is an estimate of real civilisations or of life.

      

        
N = R★ · f_p · n_e · f_l · f_i · f_c · L

        

        

        

        
Presets: the 1961 Green Bank values and the "commonly quoted set" are repeated in secondary sources; the meeting's own record was not checked. "Data where we have it" uses the measured terms below and leaves the unknown ones where you set them. R★ is stars per year; the measured Milky Way rate of 1.65 ± 0.19 M☉ per year (Licquia & Newman 2015) is a mass, not a count.

      

      
TermHow well we know itValue and source

        
R★Measured1.65 ± 0.19 M☉/yr star formation (Licquia & Newman 2015); stars per year needs an initial mass function

        
f_pMeasured≈ 1: 0.77 small planets per GK star at 50–300 d (Burke et al. 2015); ≈ 2.5 per M dwarf at P < 200 d (Dressing & Charbonneau 2015)

        
n_eConstrainedη⊕ = 0.37–0.60 for 0.5–1.5 R⊕ in the conservative zone around 4800–6300 K stars (Bryson et al. 2021); 11 ± 4% for 1–2 R⊕ at 1–4 × Earth's flux (Petigura et al. 2013)

        
f_l, f_i, f_c, LUnknownNo data. Any value is an opinion.

      

      
      

        
One number hides the uncertainty. Following Sandberg, Drexler & Ord (2018), each term is drawn from a range instead: R★ 1–100, f_p 0.1–1, n_e 0.1–1, f_i 0.001–1, f_c 0.01–1, L 100–10¹⁰ years, all log-uniform. Their f_l comes from a log-normal model of the rate at which life starts; here f_l is a log-uniform stand-in from 10⁻ᵏ to 1, with k on the slider. Draws are seeded, so the result repeats.

        
QuantityValueFrom

This page, k = 10: P(N < 1)64%[calc]
Sandberg et al. 2018: median N0.32with their f_l model; the mean is about 27 million, which is why a single average misleads
Sandberg et al. 2018: P(N < 1)≈ 52%their priors

        
The Seager equation

        
N = N★ · F_Q · F_HZ · F_O · F_L · F_S

        
It counts planets where a biosignature gas could be detected, not civilisations (Seager 2018): stars observed, the fraction quiet, with rocky planets in the habitable zone, observable, with life, and whose life makes a detectable gas.

        

        

        
Starting values: N★ = 30,000 M dwarfs bright enough for JWST, F_Q · F_HZ = 0.15, F_O = 0.001, F_L = 1, F_S = 0.5, giving N ≈ 2. They come from secondary summaries of Seager's talk and paper, not checked against the paper here; F_L = 1 is an assumption, not a measurement. The habitable-zone fraction links to the Population chapter's figures.

History and papers

      
Key papers and milestones, summarised in our own words. Each links to its paper (DOI) and to the part of SetuHQ it relates to.

      
  1. 1992
    Wolszczan & Frail
    A planetary system around the millisecond pulsar PSR B1257+12
    Two planets found from tiny delays in a dead star's radio pulses.
    The first confirmed planets beyond the Solar System.
    Wolszczan & Frail 1992, Nature 355, 145Related ›
  2. 1995
    Mayor & Queloz
    A Jupiter-mass companion to a solar-type star
    51 Pegasi b, a giant on a 4-day orbit, found from its star's wobble.
    The first planet around a Sun-like star; Nobel Prize 2019.
    Mayor & Queloz 1995, Nature 378, 355Related ›
  3. 2000
    Charbonneau et al.; Henry et al.
    HD 209458 b seen in transit
    Two teams independently caught the same planet crossing its star.
    The first transiting planet: a radius, a density, and a way into atmospheres.
    Charbonneau et al. 2000, ApJ 529, L45 (HD 209458 b)Related ›
  4. 2000
    Seager & Sasselov
    Theoretical transmission spectra during extrasolar giant planet transits
    Predicted how starlight filtered through a planet's limb would carry sodium and potassium features.
    The blueprint for transmission spectroscopy.
    Seager & Sasselov 2000, ApJ 537, 916Related ›
  5. 2002
    Charbonneau et al.
    Detection of an extrasolar planet atmosphere
    Sodium absorption in HD 209458 b during transit, 2.3 × 10⁻⁴ deeper than the continuum.
    The first exoplanet atmosphere detected.
    Charbonneau et al. 2002, ApJ 568, 377 (sodium)Related ›
  6. 2004
    Bond et al.
    OGLE 2003-BLG-235/MOA 2003-BLG-53
    A planet with 0.4% of its star's mass revealed by a short extra brightening in a lensing event.
    The first planet found by microlensing.
    Bond et al. 2004, ApJ 606, L155Related ›
  7. 2008
    Marois et al.
    Direct imaging of multiple planets orbiting the star HR 8799
    Three giant planets photographed around a young star (a fourth followed in 2010).
    The first directly imaged multi-planet system.
    Marois et al. 2008, Science 322, 1348 (HR 8799)Related ›
  8. 2008
    Kalas et al.; Gáspár & Rieke 2020
    Fomalhaut b, then reinterpreted
    An optical image of a 'planet' later explained as an expanding dust cloud from a collision.
    A caution: an image can be dust.
    Kalas et al. 2008, Science 322, 1345 (Fomalhaut b)Related ›
  9. 2010
    Borucki et al.
    Kepler planet-detection mission: introduction and first results

    The start of the statistical era of exoplanets.

    Lissauer et al.; Rowe et al.

    Catalogue ›Everything that dims
    Everything that dims.
    1,011 entries, none thrown away.
    
        
    Every consensus dip of the panel, every brightening and every star's variability from the sweep, each classified by a stated rule, with its confidence, its cues and its provenance: the marks, the weights and the Sentinels' own words. Sentinels run on Claude (Anthropic) by default; other providers are supported and labelled. Probes are deterministic matched-filter detectors.
    
      
    
      
    Known planetsEverything that dims
    
      
    A first slice, stated plainly. Sector 1: 200 of the 15,898 SPOC 2-minute targets searched (Probes only; by exoplan). 200 stars searched, 200 star-sectors, 936 consensus dips reviewed. This catalogue is separate from the discovery feed. Nothing here is a new or confirmed planet. A class is what the light curve's cues suggest; there is no pixel or centroid check, so a blended binary can look like anything. The planet-candidate rule found 3 on the real light curves and 2 on flux-inverted copies of the same stars (dips turned into bumps, so real dips cannot pass): an excess of +1 (95%: −3 to +5). They are not distinguishable from noise in this slice, so they are not presented as candidates. 0 match a known TOI.
    
      
    Each class against its own null, measured on the same 200 star-sectors: what its rule finds where its signal cannot be. Dips: the flux turned upside down (a real dip becomes a bump; a real flare or pulsation maximum becomes a dip, so this null is not empty of real signals). Flares: downward events with the real dips masked. Variability: a red-noise copy of the star (AR(1) fitted to its bins) through the same rule, which needs the same best period (within 10%) in both halves of the light curve. Of its periodogram peaks not at a binary's period, 8 are coherent; unclassified are 20 longer than a half can test (coherence not tested), 5 at the edge of the period grid and 3 that wander between halves. Limits: it finds a 300 ppm sinusoid in strong red noise only 3/20 times (scripts/variability_rule_check.py), and cannot test periods longer than about 3.8 d in one sector. Kind is compared with kind, star-sector is the unit: the 95% interval is a paired bootstrap over star-sectors, beside McNemar's test. A class that does not pass both is not distinguishable from noise in this slice: Planet candidate, Eclipsing binary, Flare, Pulsator or rotational variable, Systematic. Of the 11 flare-class brightenings, 8 rise faster than they decay and 2 the other way (1 equal); real flares rise fast, noise has no preferred direction.

    The rules, and each class against its null
    
        
    First match wins, in this order: systematic, eclipsing binary, variable, then planet candidate; a brightening is a flare unless it is systematic. The rules are in src/setuhq/variables.py and are re-applied to every contributed entry on ingest. Excess: real minus null over the same star-sectors, with a 95% interval from a paired bootstrap over star-sectors (10,000 resamples). The second table has every comparison, kind by kind.

    Explorer ›Planets
    What each depth would imply, if it were a planet.
    One card per star in the run or the feed. Each entry is a candidate, unconfirmed; the ratio below is what its stored depth implies if it were a planet.
    
      
    Radius ratio only. Rp/R* = √depth, with depth as a fraction (ppm × 10⁻⁶). This assumes a full, undiluted transit and ignores limb darkening. No stellar radius is stored in the run or the catalogue, so this page does not convert the ratio to a planet radius in Earth or Jupiter units. Each bar is a ratio scale from 0 to 0.10, the same on every card.

    Each cell: the rate, then k/n and the Wilson 95% interval. 
    The Sentinel rows cover 37 stars. Their intervals are wide, the two personas share one model (they agree on 35 of 37 stars, φ = 0.88), so they count as one correlated voter, not two, and they were never run on the control light curves. The Probes + Sentinels rows are star-level combinations of stored outcomes, stated before scoring, not a run of the panel's consensus.
    Rules
    1. Scored on the held-out half of the frozen sample only (TOIs by sha256(seed:TIC) parity); the tuning half is never scored.
    2. A submission lists, for every star of its scope, the events its method detected on the real light curve and on the flux-inverted and block-scrambled controls (time, duration, period, its own pass verdict and flags). The leaderboard decides which events lie on the TOI's ephemeris (the benchmark's score_star and match_toi) and counts control false alarms itself. Self-reported outcomes are not accepted.
    3. Rank: Youden's J on the searchable set the benchmark fixed (stars with a SPOC 2-minute light curve), with one predicate on both sides, a clean candidate (on the ephemeris, passed, no eclipsing-binary flag): J = the share of CP/KP stars offered as clean candidates + the share of FP stars not offered − 1, with a square-and-add Wilson interval. Calling every TOI a planet, with or without a flag, scores J = 0; a searchable star called not searched counts as not offered. J over every star of the scope is shown beside it. Where intervals overlap, the order is not a measured difference.
    4. The controls gate ranking and do not enter J: only held-out entries with both control lists on every searched star are ranked, others are listed unranked. The control lists are the method's own report; the leaderboard cannot recompute them without the light curves. The Sentinel subsample is never ranked.
    5. A floor: the metadata-only baseline uses no light curve at all, only the public TOI number, period, duration, ephemeris errors and epoch, with a logistic regression fitted on the tuning half. A method that does not beat it is not shown to read the light curves better than the catalogue's own metadata predicts dispositions.
    6. A submission states the sha256 of the public inputs it was built from (tuning half with labels, held-out half without). Any other hash, tuned_on other than none or tuning, a field outside the whitelist, a missing or extra star, or missing provenance: refused, with the reasons listed.
    7. The hash is an attestation: the held-out labels are public in the repository, so the leaderboard cannot prove they were not read, and a method's pass verdicts and control events are its own report. Maintainer-held decoy light curves and prospective scoring on TOIs still undispositioned would close these gaps; neither exists yet.
    8. FP rejection: FP stars whose TOI dip the method did not offer as a clean candidate (recovered and not flagged). Reliability: the share of clean candidates on TOI dips that are CP/KP, on this sample's class mix, which is not the TOI catalogue's. All rates carry Wilson 95% intervals. TFOPWG dispositions are the reference, not ground truth for every TOI.
    9. Measured on a stated benchmark; nothing on this leaderboard is a discovery.
    Submission format and refusal rules: docs/leaderboard/README.md. Score a submission with setuhq leaderboard <file>.
